<reason>PRO built a memorable case on honest pricing, fairness, and accountability, but CON steadily narrowed the debate to a single question PRO could not win: does the motion actually leave servers better paid? CON's Meyer example, the tip-versus-service-charge legal distinction, the hours-volatility turn, and especially the full-minimum-plus-tips states test (servers who already have a wage floor still keep tips) were grounded, plausible, and never squarely answered—PRO's "arbitrage" reply fits the one-restaurant case but not those states, and the "larger for the median" claim was asserted without support. Under pressure PRO conceded the $30/hr server takes a cut and then, in closing, that "honest prices are smaller than dishonest ones," which CON converted into a clean decision rule against a motion that promises higher base pay. PRO retained a live route on customer transparency and the boss-plus-table-nine framing, and CON's three clipped turns are a real execution cost, so this stays competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B4.4–B4.6 / B5.1: taking PRO's honest answer to "name the number" and reframing it—"predictability of a pay cut is still a pay cut... the one number PRO can commit to is the one that goes down"—then locking it in when PRO's closing conceded honest prices are smaller.</best_rebuttal>
